newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NAB SAYS LENDING MARGINS STABILISING.
newsitem.headline: NAB SAYS LENDING MARGINS STABILISING.

text.p: National Australia Bank Ltd managing director Don Argus said on Monday that lending margins were stabilising in the current fourth quarter of the year to September 30, 1997.
Argus also said that his original target of a 40 percent cost-to-income ratio by the year 2000 would take a little longer to achieve because of the Millennium Bug costs.
He said he would advise the market in three to four weeks time on the cost to the bank of dealing with the Millennium Bug.

"No, I wouldn't think (margins have eroded further) in our place," Argus told reporters after a luncheon address to the Securities Institute. He had been asked if margins were eroding further in the fourth quarter.
"At this stage, the margin erosion is stabilised," he said.

"But again, we have to compete, and if somebody does something on price then we're not going to lose any customers," he said. Earlier Argus told the luncheon margins in the fourth quarter results would not disappoint.
In late July Argus said after releasing flat third quarter profit results that there was continued pressure on margins.
Argus said he was still committed to the target of reducing costs to 40 percent of income.
NAB's cost-to-income ratio stood at 54.8 percent at June 30.
Argus earlier told the luncheon that he Aood by his oft-repeated target of a 40 percent ratio despite the costs of changing computer systems to deal with the Millennium problem.
"The 40 percent stake in the ground is still real -- it's still there," he said.
But his earlier target of 40 percent by the year 2000 may have been too ambitious, he said.
"That's going to take time to get as we reinvest and deal with the year 2000 issue," he said.
"I wanted it by the year 2000, but you've got to deal with the Year 2000 technology issues around the globe so it will be a little longer, but not too much longer," he said.
The Reserve Bank of Australia said in June that the Year 2000 Millenium bug could cost Australia's four largest banks more than A$350 million.
Argus earlier told the luncheon NAB remained very acquisitive and that observers should not be surprised if it formed new alliances to distribute its products.
He said significant organic growth took too long to achieve.
NAB's preferred target markets for acquisitions were Australia, the United States, Britain and Ireland. The Asian region was also a target market, he said.
Argus denied that the prices for United States financial institutions had risen too high.

"No. The U.S. is a tremendous market to be in. It's the most dynamic market we're in at the moment and when you've got GDP growth of five percent and unemployment of four percent, why wouldn't you want to be there."

There has been some speculation that NAB failed in a bid to buy U.S. credit card group Advanta Corp because the price was too high and that NAB had shifted its focus away from the United States because of the high prices.
"There'll be opportunities," he said.
-- Bernard Hickey, Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
